utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon. We're ready to continue with the evidence of Mr. Sljivancanin. I would remind you, Mr. Sljivancanin, of the affirmation that you made at the beginning of your evidence which still applies. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to all the participants in these proceedings. Mr. Sljivancanin, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If you remember correctly, on Friday, if I can put it that way, we sort of rounded off your testimony with the end of your stay in Vukovar, so I would actually like to add a few questions to that very shortly. Do you remember when you returned from Vukovar? Did you return together with your unit and if so, do you remember the date?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember it was a Sunday and the date was the 24th of November, 1991. I returned around 2200 hours to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now we are going to look at a few more documents. These are your reports. So we're going to comment on those reports. Before that, we spoke about your reports generally and we looked at them too. How often did you send reports from the Vukovar front that went to the assistant for security at the SSNO and to the security administration? How often were these reports written?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: These reports were written or sent sometimes every three days, sometimes every other day, depending on the information gathered and the needs involved in terms of my reporting.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On Friday, when you described that telephone conversation with the security administration in the evening of the 20th of November, you testified about that. In relation to that oral conversation, did you write a written report about that or not?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The day I testified, you interrupted me. After the TV programme was over, I went to the premises where the security organ was and I wrote a report regarding security which I sent on the 21st of November to Belgrade. In that report, as far as I can remember, I briefly described what I did or, rather, what the security organs did, and I also wrote that part of the suspects, the crime suspects that were brought to the barracks were taken over by the government of Slavonia, Baranja and Western Srem.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, now, I would like to look at two or three documents. Could two of them go -- be dealt with in private session because a witness is being referred to that requires private session. So could we please just deal with that in private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We're confused, Mr. Lukic, whether the document should be under seal or in public. You dealt with it in private but the content doesn't seem to be ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm afraid -- well, perhaps we could wait for the break and then I will check. I'm afraid that when we questioned a certain witness during our cross-examination that we asked him about certain facts from this document, so in that sense, perhaps it should be under seal because that was in public session. So perhaps -- but if you like, I can check that part of the transcript during the break and then I can come back to you with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. We will just leave that for the moment, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The next document is a document marked -- I mean from the 65 ter list, it is 15, so it can be dealt with in public; 3D050066. It is a document that is entitled "Use of Units of the Military Police in Carrying Out Combat Activities," dated the 10th of December, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sljivancanin, just in a word or two, not to analyse the document, who is the author of this document and who was it sent to and for what purpose?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am the author of this document as well. After returning -- after the units returned from carrying out their mission in Vukovar, it says here, on the 10th of December, 1991, at the request of the chief of the security administration, I wrote my own positions and views with regard to using the units of the military police in combat activities and my proposals as to what should be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That does belong to the duties of the security organs, using the military police and proposing measures for using the military police; right?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is one of the tasks involved in the specialist direction of the military police and of security organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we get a number for this document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 841, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The last document that I wish to analyse now -- again, for a moment, I would like to move into private session, and then we are going to take a position as to whether this document can later be exhibited in public because of part of its content. This is a document that is also from the 65 ter list and I think it is number 16. It's the document numbered 3D050070. It is a document also addressed to the security administration. It is entitled, "The Course of Combat Activities in the Fighting for Vukovar." The date is the 10th of December, 1991.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: "The Liberation of Vukovar." Interpreter's note: We do not have any of these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] During the break, I'm going to check this out and I'm also going to consult Mr. Moore to see what his position is regarding these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sljivancanin, let's move on to another subject and then let's draw this to a close. You heard the testimony of Mrs. Florence Hartmann; there's no problem mentioning her name now. Were you in Vukovar in 1992? And did you talk to her? And why did you go to Vukovar then? You remember what her evidence was.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard here the testimony of Madam Florence Hartmann, and, to tell you the truth, I was surprised. I was in Vukovar in 1991 but not in order to celebrate. I went to pay my respects to the victims, especially two young men who got killed as they were helping me to get out the body of my late driver, Popovic. And I went straight to the cemetery in Vukovar. I did not meet with anyone, but I believe that I would have remembered the lady, had I met her. I first saw her here in this courtroom, and before that I saw her once on television. I read the words that she said here in her notebook. It is correct that I said then that "This is Yugoslavia and this is Montenegro," when I made a statement for Radio Vukovar, because many were provoking me and asking me how I could come without a passport. I never had a passport and I did not have it even when I was brought to The Hague. I believe that she recorded these words in her notebook from that statement because it was broadcast several times on that day in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In view of the documents that we have seen here before this Court, obviously, towards the end of 1992, the media started talking about the discovery of the mass grave at Ovcara. When did you hear about this event and about the story about Ovcara, and what was your position at that time when you heard about it?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Regarding your first question, I forgot. At that time, I had collected some money and I took it to the children of these killed people who were salvaging my driver, and that was one of the principal reasons why I was going to Vukovar at that time. As regards your second question which you have just put to me, the media at the time carried a lot of misinformation. In fact, I did not read much of the press at the time, especially not the so-called yellow press. I did not believe that something of the kind could happen, nor could have happened, nor did I know that anything of the kind had happened. And, as sometime in 1993, I went to Podgorica, there was less talk about it there. I actually did not believe the press, what was being said in the papers, and I didn't pay much attention to it then.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I shall now ask you something about the statements that you gave to the security administration and before the military court. Please be so kind as to give me brief answers so that we can go through this quickly. Probably the OTP will have some other questions in that connection and we shall leave that to them. You were called - I believe that I can, in fact, be leading when asking you this question - in February 1998 to the security administration. My question is: When you went for that talk on the 14th of February, were you told what the reason for your having been called to that talk was?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In February 1998, I attended the National Defence School as a trainee. It was Saturday; I remember that well. The chief of the centre called me and he gave me the phone to talk to the Chief of Staff, General Perisic. So I took it and I called him and he said that I was to go to the chief of security, Aca Dmitrijevic, the chief in the security administration. I didn't know why. When I arrived there, General Aca Dmitrijevic told me that we were to talk about the events in Vukovar, actually, what I knew at that point in time about Vukovar. And he assigned Colonel Branko Gajic to talk to me and he conducted this interview with me all day, from 11.00 a.m. to, perhaps, 1900 hours. I cannot remember with precision, but it took the whole day. That, I know for a fact. I asked him to give me the reports that I was writing at the time and had written prior to that, because I could not recall all the details, or to let me go and find the notebook of mine. Mr. Gajic told me that it wasn't necessary; that it was important that I tell him what I knew about it. And he asked me not to make any references to any names, except Mr. Mrksic, Mr. Radic and me, myself, and some people that were there working with me, because they were referred to in the indictment of the Tribunal at The Hague, and that I should not be calling out any other names.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On that occasion, were you read the indictment of the OTP of the Tribunal at The Hague?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were you presented at that time any material from that period - any orders, reports, working diaries, notebooks, statements by persons?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, nothing of the kind was presented to me, although I asked them to give me at least a couple of my own documents that I had written in order for me to remember certain things. But I was given no material.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was it made possible for you to consult any attorney, any lawyer, at that time in connection with the topics that were being discussed?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was not. I said, the moment I arrived there for talks, we started and I had to stay there until 7.00 p.m. And actually, I said much more than is contained in this official memorandum which was dictated by an official and he actually dictated more things that he wanted to go into that statement than my very words.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Upon finishing that conversation, were you given a copy of the statement for you to keep?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No statement was given to me. That statement was not given to me. In fact, after I finished -- I had finished my account, we had a bit of an argument, so to speak, because I said that I wouldn't go on talking anymore as the gentleman was insisting on putting things down the way he saw fit, without any references to any names that were crucial in certain terms; people from the security administration who had been coming to Vukovar and that of Mr. Aca Vasiljevic. So I said that I was going to leave the office, that I was hungry, that I could no longer listen to that. I told them, "Give me what you have to sign," and I didn't even read, frankly speaking, what it was that I was signing.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sometime in the winter of that year, you also were heard before the military court in the capacity of witness, which statement will probably be presented to you as well. Let me ask you a couple of questions connected to that particular procedure. First of all, on that occasion, as we can see from the transcript, The Hague investigators, the OTP's investigators, were also there. Were you handed the indictment of the Tribunal at The Hague?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember it having -- that it was handed over to me, the indictment, that is. I remember that I received a summons for appearing before the court and I arrived in the court. Having arrived there, I waited for a while in the waiting room; then they ushered me in. I took the stand and immediately the giving of my testimony started.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You don't remember whether an indictment was given to you. Do you remember whether the indictment was retold to you; and if so, were you given any time to give it some thought prior to beginning to make your own statement?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that in the introductory remarks, when the judge was introducing the case, he said that I had been summoned in connection with The Hague indictment about events at Ovcara in 1991. I believe that that is how he ushered in the case. And he said that people from the Tribunal at The Hague were present and, as far as I can recall, they were sitting to my right-hand side, three of them. Then the questions immediately started, and I replied to the questions being put to me by his honour, the judge, and I do not remember any other details. It goes without saying that what I was telling them, he then retold -- re-dictated to the typist in his own words and he typed it down.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On that day, before the examination, during the examination, did you get from the examining magistrate any material associated with the indictment, any document? Were you given or shown any document by anyone when your statement was being taken?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one gave me any materials or any documents associated with the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On that occasion, did anyone read you your rights as a person accused before the Tribunal at The Hague, according to the Statute of this Tribunal then?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, there was no mention of it at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sljivancanin, when you stated your first views, so to speak, on the indictment, which was in the summer, I believe, of 1993, do you -- 2003 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear counsel, who could kindly slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- were you given any documents? Do you remember that? Would you repeat, sir, when you were giving -- when you were stating -- making your plea as to your guilt before this Tribunal, do you remember whether you got any accompanying/supporting material with the indictment?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that I did get such material. I was without counsel then, so that people here in the courtroom actually gave it to me. I do remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Had you seen that material ever before?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw those materials for the first time when I arrived here.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm drawing to a close my examination. I wanted us to go in details through the specific paragraphs of the indictment, but I believe that we have dealt with a lot of those through your testimony. Mr. Sljivancanin, when you were stating your plea in connection with this indictment of this Tribunal and before your first initial appearance, and also later when the indictment was amended, you pled not guilty. You are now speaking under oath and I am asking you, in connection with just one topic, one subject, because I believe we have dealt with the other topics so far. You have read the indictment. You see that it is the contention of the OTP that you are a participant in the joint criminal enterprise with inter alia Mr. Mrksic and Radic and other known and unknown persons whose goal was to persecute non-Serbs from the Vukovar Hospital after the fall of Vukovar by way of murder and extermination. This is, of course, a paraphrase but you know what my question is: Did you know of any enterprise, of any agreement, to commit this crime as stated in the indictment, and did you participate in it?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Many of these things in the indictment have been written arbitrarily and as someone saw fit. First and foremost, I never participated in any agreements or enterprises. Mr. Mrksic was my superior and I had a professional position vis-a-vis all the tasks that he gave me. He never issued me any order which was in contravention of the law, nor did he ever require anything of the kind from me. And then I would not have executed any order that would have been outside the ambit of my duty. Mr. Radic was a company commander and I saw him, I mean, tour the company, the front line, several times, just as I did the other commanders. I never issued him any orders, nor did he have any need to associate with me in regard of any question. He had his own superior commanding officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you hear that such an agreement existed between any persons while you were there in the territory of Vukovar for the commission of such a crime?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only heard about anything of the kind from this indictment that I read here for the first time, and I know that there were never any such agreements at that time. Had there been any such deals being made, we would have taken measures to prevent them, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have finished with my examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sljivancanin, would you like to add something which you believe I have, perhaps, omitted to ask and which you believe is of importance and should be stated here before the Trial Chamber, and relates to the events we discussed the last three days?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I should like to ask the Chamber, if it is necessary - and I am endeavouring to be as brief as possible and not to tire everybody - perhaps they will ask me something about what I wanted to say, so if I could ask the Trial Chamber to ask me their questions, and if I feel that I haven't been asked that crucial question, then I shall say it myself, by your leave, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You heard what Mr. Radic had to say to the Trial Chamber prior to redirect, but I should like to ask you to say what it is that you want to say before this Tribunal. Of course, they will be topics that will be the subject of redirect and cross-examination as well.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If there is something that I wish to say, this is something which distresses me the most as a human being; the fact that I should feature in this kind of an indictment, and that the crime which was conceived of, as I said in my introductory remarks before this august Chamber, by non-human beings, by cowards and by [Realtime transcript read in error "my"] psychopaths in order to tarnish the prestige and the dignity of all of us who loved Yugoslavia and of all members of the Yugoslav Peoples' Army who honourably discharged what they had pledged to, in order to inflict great pain and suffering on the families of the victims. Thinking whether I should take the stand, I decided that I, indeed, should sit in this chair and say the truth about everything that I know in order not to have the reputation and dignity of the honourable members of the Yugoslav Peoples' Army tarnished, that of me, myself, and that of my family; and also in order to respond to all those who have used the media in a bid to present many things untruthfully; so that I could tell what the truth is; and also, when it comes to the families of the people who were unfortunately killed at Ovcara, to tell their families what it is that I know and to try and, if at all possible, alleviate their pain, to tell them what I know. I am here. I have taken the stand. I am at your disposal. Please ask me all and any questions. I will say everything that I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On page 16, there is a correction, line 16. The transcript says "my psychopaths" and, of course, the witness has just said "psychopaths." Thank you, Your Honours, I have finished with my examination-in-chief at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I possibly ask the Court's indulgence for 15 minutes, for the Court to rise for 15 minutes. It's for the following reason: Files have been prepared for cross-examination. There was a typographical error, or errors, and I want to make absolutely certain that it has been done properly so that when we commence - and I believe we may commence in cross-examination on behalf of the Prosecution - sooner rather than later, then there will not be the danger of any problems, and that perhaps 15 minutes spent now will ensure that there will be no difficulties later on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You want this before we hear from Mr. Vasic and Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I just wanted to make sure that if there was any error, if there was any error, that it would be dealt with now when there's cross-examination going on that does not relate to us. Otherwise, it would be not desirable for documents to be in the wrong position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, is it your intention to put questions to the witness? It is?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon. Indeed, it is. I don't have too many questions, but yes, I will have questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I think I will need about ten minutes, also. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Moore, the members of the Chamber are not altogether clear about your concern. In view of what Mr. Vasic and Mr. Borovic have said, do you still feel the break now is important?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: There are 32 documents that have been put into a file and there are three other files. I want to make absolutely certain that they are accurate. There have been problems with the machines upstairs in relation to the documents going through for those files. I could leave it, quite clearly, until the conclusion of Mr. Borovic's cross-examination. Then I would hope we would have reached the break, but we would not have the time to use -- to repair or to alter anything. I would like to have the documents to start immediately because that way, then, the cross-examination can flow without any fear of interruption. As I said, the machine, unfortunately, has jumped at some paper and has created problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will take our first break now and resume at half past 3.00, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just thank the Court for the time. We have the documents, and perhaps I prayed a little harder today than normal, but they're all available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If we've managed to get you to do that, we have achieved a great deal in the interests of humanity, Mr. Moore. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I conducted some checks but I can only tell you about them in private session, about the documents that we spoke of earlier.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone in the courtroom. Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, Mr. Sljivancanin. Witness, good afternoon. I am going to ask you the same thing that Mr. Lukic asked you; namely, to make a brief pause after my question and I will do the same after your answer so that the interpretation service can interpret our dialogue and so that everything can be recorded properly. Thank you. First of all, I'd like to start with a topic where I think there was a slip of the tongue in your evidence, and it has to do with Colonel Pavkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see on our screens Exhibit 404, which is the order that instructed Colonel Pavkovic to go to Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: As we are waiting for this document, let me ask you: Do you know that in 1991, during this period of time, what was the post held by Colonel Pavkovic?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Nebojsa Pavkovic was Deputy Chief of Staff of the Federal Secretary or Federal Minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You said Federal Secretary of ...

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: National Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Based on the order that we can see on our screens, it was precisely the Federal Secretary who had sent Colonel Pavkovic to Negoslavci, and in item 4 of this report -- of this order, it says that Colonel Pavkovic is expected to send reports, observations, and proposals to the cabinet of the Federal Secretary. Does this mean that Colonel Pavkovic, at the time, was sent there as some kind of a supervisor, somebody who is supposed to check how things were going, as a representative of the Superior Command?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that Mr. Pavkovic was in Negoslavci throughout the entire time; that he cooperated with Mr. Mrksic; and that very frequently he acted as a sort of a supervisor, somebody who was there to control the work of others. He was the only one authorised to give any sort of criticism to Colonel Mrksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Given that Colonel Pavkovic had come from the Superior Command, Colonel Mrksic was not his superior because that would have violated the chain of command and the principle of singleness of command. What Colonel Mrksic could do, though, was to entrust him with certain tasks upon prior agreement with him.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pursuant to the regulations that were in force in the Yugoslav Peoples' Army at the time, since Pavkovic came from the Superior Command, it is true that Mrksic was unable to issue any assignments to him. However, they were able to carry out many assignments in cooperation, upon prior agreement between the two of them. Naturally, there should have been, perhaps, an instruction from the Federal Secretary or the Chief of Staff of the Federal Secretary, and I had nothing to do with that. It was completely outside of my responsibilities. But he could have supervised how the implementation of these assignments was conducted.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. While we're still dealing with Colonel Pavkovic, and in relation to something you gave about here, namely, the evacuation of the Vukovar Hospital, I would like to see Exhibit 314 on our screens, please, page -- with ERN number 04687773.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While we're waiting, let me clarify. This is an excerpt from the notes of Mr. Kypr, which was the notebook used by Mr. Lukic yesterday. This is a different excerpt from that notebook. No, that's not the right page. 04687773. This is an entry --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I apologise, but Exhibit 314 has only got one page and it's the one currently displayed on the screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that case, I need to apologise. I was given a wrong reference. Just a minute, please. I need to verify the number under which this was filed; namely, the diary of Mr. Kypr. While we're looking for the number, let me just explain what this concerns. This is an entry made by Mr. Kypr - the exhibit number is 344, I apologise - namely, this is an entry about Colonel Pavkovic saying that the wounded members of paramilitary formations need to remain here and that it was ultimately resolved with General Raseta. This page is going to come up. This is page 04687773. Can we please zoom in on the first portion.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sljivancanin, do you see this entry at the very beginning of the page?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see the page but I can't read anything on it, nor do I understand what's written on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I'm going to try and read this out and then you can follow. "The wounded members of paramilitary formations need to remain here. This was definitely resolved with General Raseta." Do you know anything about the conversations between General Raseta and Colonel Pavkovic regarding this?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time Colonel Pavkovic never informed me, nor did he tell me about any conversations he had with anyone else, because he was from the Superior Command. Now, as to whether he informed Colonel Mrksic about this or not, I don't know. You need to ask the two of them about that. Now, another matter that has to do with the chain of command and with relations that existed between them, item 35 of the rules of service in the armed forces specifies that, in a particular area or in a garrison or in the barracks, the most senior officer is the one so designated by the commander. If Colonel Mrksic had received an order, which I didn't see, from the commander of the Military District about him being the commander, then, in terms of discipline, he was able to specify certain rules for everyone, including Colonel Pavkovic. I know for a fact that Colonel Pavkovic frequently contacted the Chief of Staff, the chef du cabinet, of the Federal Secretary and some generals from the General Staff. And as for what kind of orders and assignments he received from them, I know nothing about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'd like to turn to another topic which, once again, has to do with the evidence you gave; namely, when you mentioned that the commissioner of the Croatian government for Vukovar called the command in Negoslavci at one point in time, and that a meeting with Colonel Mrksic was scheduled for the following day, in the afternoon, and that you were informed of the substance of these talks; namely, the conditions of surrender which Colonel Mrksic, in your words, conveyed to the Croatian government commissioner. I'd like to know whether these conditions of surrender pertained to the entire paramilitary forces of Croatia, those which were in the inner urban area, including Borovo Naselje, since Mitnica had been cut off the minute the units of the JNA took that area.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know for a fact that Colonel Mrksic spoke sometime in the morning, at around 9.00, or perhaps even earlier, at 8.00. At any rate, it was not yet 10.00 in the morning. I know that he talked to Mr. Vidic and that he dictated to him very specific conditions for surrender. I was present when they talked. I listened to that conversation. Later on, Mr. Mrksic said that he hesitated and that he wasn't sure that everybody would agree to those conditions and that he would let him know later on. I know that this pertained to the forces which were in the central area of Vukovar and in the area towards the hospital. I can't be sure that Borovo Naselje was included because I didn't listen on. Colonel Mrksic had the phone in his hands. But I remember when Colonel Mrksic said that all those with weapons need to go to the stadium - and I told you that I could point that stadium out - and that if they surrendered and dropped their weapons, not a hair would be harmed on their heads. And as far as I remember, at least not to my knowledge, there were no further contacts with Marin Vidic. He did not call later on, and if I am mistaken, then Colonel Mrksic can tell you what he knows.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: We heard from many witnesses here about what happened after members of these paramilitary formations went to the hospital; namely, some went to the hospital and some left Vukovar. I'd like to know whether you know when the commander of the Vukovar defence, called Mladi Jastreb, left Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know based on my talks with Mrs. Vesna Bosanac and Mr. Marin Vidic. I inquired, I said that I wanted to meet those people because I knew that they had been officers of the Yugoslav Peoples' Army, and I wanted to see what was it that prompted them to fire at each other and to kill our own soldiers, those that we had trained together with until recently. And this is what Mrs. Vesna Bosanac told me: "You will never find the two of them. They had escaped from Vukovar five days ago. Don't look for them. The only ones who remained faithful to this town and to these people are Marin Vidic and myself. There are others as well who didn't manage to flee. They changed their clothes and they hid in the hospital. I will point out those people to you. And as for when he left, I truly don't know that." Later on, in the evening, Marin Vidic, when talking, confirmed the same thing that Mrs. Vesna Bosanac said. And, coincidently, as I have quite a lot of time available to me here in prison, I frequently watch Croatian television; they have good programmes and I understand the language. And last year, I watched a TV programme - it was the anniversary of the liberation of Vukovar - and there were two men in that programme, including some other people who wrote books about Vukovar, and these same questions were put to both of these men as to when they had left Vukovar and why. This gentleman, who was nicknamed Mladi Jastreb, if I can say so, was barely able to stutter that he had left before the 17th, but he wouldn't give the precise date as to when he had left. That's all I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that you talked to Marin Vidic and Vesna Bosanac. Are you familiar with the details surrounding the attempt of Marin Vidic to negotiate the surrender with Goran Hadzic, who, at the time, was the Prime Minister of Eastern Slavonia, Baranja and Western Srem, and immediately prior to the fall of Vukovar, which is to say, from the 15th to the 18th of November?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I talked to Mr. Marin Vidic, he was a man prepared to say many a thing. We had come to a sort of meeting of minds, to a common position; namely, we thought -- both thought that it was ugly that things should have come to that point where combat operations had to be carried out. And I believe I think -- I remember that there was this attempt, but the meeting did not come about. I cannot remember why not. But he gave me three letters which he had written to the president of -- the then President of the Republic of Croatia, Mr. Franjo Tudjman, and I submitted those letters to the security administration. In these letters, he described in detail that it was not good that there should have been armed combat. He wrote how a lieutenant of the Yugoslav Peoples' Army had been killed who had come to a session of the municipality, the municipal assembly of Vukovar. He was an assemblyman and he came to this assembly session in Vukovar in 1991, after which session he was treacherously killed. He told me the following: In his view, the army had also done wrong, and it was wrong, as he put it, three times. The first time was in August, in the month of August, when the army entered the city and was able to control the city and all of a sudden, it just withdrew. I wasn't there then. I don't know why it withdrew. The second time it was remiss was between the -- was the period between the 2nd and 10th of October, when they felt that a disciplined and strong unit was there; and the minute they wanted to lay down their arms, the army stopped. I remember that -- I remember that. And we stopped because we had received orders to the effect that all combat operations were to cease, that the convoy be let into Vukovar. And we had no combat operations, we did not conduct anything until the 20th. The third time it was wrong, he said, was when the army stopped, on the 10th of November, having reach Milovo Brdo. Then, again, they also wanted to lay down their arms but we stopped because we had no troops, because the reserve force had left. We had discharged many volunteers for lack of discipline and we were afraid lest we be surrounded. And this is what the Mr. Marin Vidic personally told me in this talk that we conducted. I can say here publicly that he treated me very fair and that the conversation that we had was a very correct one. Also, he told me this, when I asked him, "Why did you burn our soldiers?" And I have to say to this distinguished and honourable Chamber that, of the ten people who went missing and we couldn't find, I only found five burned bodies, their five bodies, in the street of Sremski Boraca. They also showed me six mounds. I asked Mr. Vidic why these bodies had been burned, and he told me this: At a certain meeting, President Tudjman had told them that the then well-known Serbian nationalist Vuk Draskovic had said that the borders of Serbia would be where Serb graves are, and it was ordered that they should not be, therefore, buried but burned. I was really surprised by that, but I presumed that he was telling the truth. And he gave me his log, his diary, in which he had written that down, which diary I then handed over to the security administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Please tell me, on that occasion, did he tell you that the session of the government of the Republic of Croatia discussed, on the 17th of November, whether to allow Mr. Vidic to negotiate with Goran Hadzic or not? Did he tell you anything about that particular issue?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time he had numerous objections levelled at the leadership and top of the Croatian government and authorities. He had the most criticism for Mr. Tudjman. I cannot remember all the details, but I know that he had a lot of objections levelled against the conduct of the Croatian leadership, and, as he put it, then he was in favour of a peaceful coexistence of all the people who were living in Vukovar then. This is what he told me and I believe that that is also what he meant, that he really believed in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your testimony, we saw some footage in which you also touched upon the question of the relationship of the JNA vis-a-vis the civilians - women, children, and the elderly - and, in fact, the desire of the JNA for the women, children, and the elderly to be taken out of Vukovar already in October 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should now like to ask that we take a look at video 1D42, the mark it bears. It is from a Croatian television programme called Latinica. We have a technical glitch. Just a minute. Obviously this is a major technical problem, or at least more than I thought. Let us go to another topic and hopefully we shall be able to see this video a bit later.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: In the examination-in-chief, you spoke about the establishment of the Operations Group South --

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I started dealing with another topic but then the video started. Obviously, we can't continue with that so I'll resume this subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: So you spoke about Operations Group South and you presented your position as part of the units which were at the Vukovar front line at that time. I should like to know whether you were there during the change-over of duty between the command of the Operations Group command -- the Operations Group South command, led by Bajo Bojat, and the command of the Guards Motorised Brigade, headed by Commander Milan Mrksic, because, in the war log, the entry for the 8th of October states that there, indeed, was such a change-over of duty.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that the -- I said that I remember that for a while the commander was Bajo Bojat and the Chief of Staff was Ljubicic, and that they were accommodated in a house on the outskirts of Negoslavci, in the direction of Vukovar, closer to there. In the initial days of the combat operations, I very often was, as I have said, on the front line because of my operational duties, and I really do not remember having attended such a meeting. I cannot recall one. Perhaps one was held. If it is entered in the war log, it probably took place, but I cannot remember having attended it. What I do remember is that on one occasion I attended a meeting when General Zivota Panic came, when I was supposed to bring Lieutenant Colonel Novakovic from the barracks in order for them to explain to him that he was no longer independent but shall be subordinated to Commander Mrksic. But I didn't manage to do that and General Panic later just removed that lieutenant colonel, so to speak, from that zone. This is what I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember whether certain chiefs of the services and branches within the command of the Guards Brigade were issued orders that they would be thereafter chiefs of the services and branches of the Operations Group, or was this dealt with by a change-over document? What do you know about this?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I know is that we worked the most and devoted the most attention to the discharge of the task of lifting the blockade on the barracks and the disarming of the paramilitary units in the city of Vukovar, and that task, as you can see, by the orders and commands here, was carried out by the Guards Brigade in conjunction with the Territorial Defence detachment of Vukovar. I don't know whether the other chiefs had any powers, and what powers they had. They knew what their duty and work was. But I never received any orders, nor did I know that I was the chief of security of Operations Group South. And let me emphasise, also, according to the rules of service, the work of security organs does not involve specialised direction in ad hoc formations, in terms of the work of security organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Tell me, from what we hear now, it emanates that -- it stems that the chief of the security organ in the Guards Brigade only dealt with units of the Guards Brigade. Who discharged this work in other units which were part of the Operations Group South? And where was the singleness of control and command established with these units in terms of the specialised direction of security organs; at which level, namely?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Organs of security are not units; these are specialised command organs, organs of the command. The organ of security of the brigade is subordinated to the commander of the brigade. I tried to familiarise myself with the entire security situation in the zone of operations or zone of responsibility, what you will, of the Guards Motorised Brigade. Every chief of security of other units also had to be informed and had to inform their commanders, and, according to the specialised technical line of duty, they were to be issued certain tasks in terms of counter-intelligence, estimates, evaluations, and their work from -- would be directed by the organs of the Superior Command in terms of counter-intelligence work. Next, units which were deployed, which came to the area of Vukovar, changed very quickly; units from the 1st Military District, namely. I'm talking about the 453rd Mechanised Brigade. It was, therefore, a very short stint. The Nubia -- the Podunavska Brigade, only for 10 days or so; the 20th Partisan Brigade, some 10 to 20 days or so; and then the 80th Motorised Brigade came which was to inherit that zone from us. It was not -- there was no possibility for establishing any counter-intelligence work and to direct it in any specialised or technical manner with such organs. They are not separate organs which are something separate from the line of duty of their particular unit. This is what I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Does this mean that these units which were outside the Guards Brigade, were, in fact, not covered by counter-intelligence in this period during which there was no, as you call it, specialist direction line? Does that mean that?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that does not mean that. It means that it was the territory of the 1st Military District on which they probably had also certain counter-intelligence groups, so to call them. Evidence about that has been given here by Dragoljub Vukosavljevic, the chief of security of the 80th Motorised Brigade, who said that he had met some people from those groups. He said so here. But throughout my stay in that terrain, I never met those people or such people, except on the 19th, in the evening, with those who had come there with permission to perform specific tasks. They had specialist direction from their own superior security organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You mean those officers from the security administration and from the security department of the 1st Military District, I assume?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I primarily mean the professional organs of security that from the 1st Military District that were somewhere in the area of Sid. I don't know where they were exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you have any knowledge whatsoever about these groups that came from Sid? We heard that from Witness Vukosavljevic without any doubt. They came to the Vukovar front. How long did they stay? What were their tasks? Or did you not know anything about this?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did our best to establish full security in the zone of activity of the Guards Brigade; however, you cannot have policemen at every corner and you cannot have them monitoring who is moving about where. Different people could have come as civilians, whatever. No one reported to me and I did not have any knowledge of any one of my security organs having any kind of contact with such persons during our stay in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Tell me, according to the rules of your profession, an officer who comes from a counter-intelligence group, would he have to report to the security organ on the territory to which he came?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already said that this was the territory controlled by units of the 1st Military District. That was their territorial jurisdiction. We came for a concrete task and that task of ours was the task of the Guards Brigade; namely, to deblock the barracks and to disarm paramilitary formations in the town of Vukovar. It was not their duty to report to us and to tell us what they were doing in the field of counter-intelligence, nor were they supposed to report to me, as the chief of security of a tactical unit, as the brigade was.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Just one more question in relation to this: The members of these counter-intelligence groups, are they also subordinated to the security administration? Is the security administration actually the organ which secures this professional unity in terms of the work of all organs?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The security administration gave professional specialist direction to the organs of the 1st Military District. The chief of security of the 1st Military District had, within his composition, intelligence groups, as far as I know. Now, how he directed them, how he guided them, how they worked, I really cannot say. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you know what kind of security organs existed in the units of the Territorial Defence of Vukovar, in the Leva Supoderica unit? Do you have any knowledge about that, whether the security organs had a network from these units?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I'm supposed to give any answers regarding the method of work of security organs, could we please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: By all means.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would kindly ask that we move into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: As for these problems of functioning, did Aca Vasiljevic, the then chief of the security administration, did he know about these problems? And you told us about when he came there. Was he aware of the situation? Did he know what the security situation was, or rather, the situation with the security organs in this area?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: When Aca Vasiljevic stayed in Vukovar, he talked to me only about security and the tasks of the security organs in the Guards Brigade, and he gave me advice as to what it was that I should do and how I could best do it. We never talked about any kind of security problems of other units, nor did I ask him anything about it or about the staffs of the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. During the examination-in-chief, you mentioned a telegram that you got, and you said that you talked to Mr. Vasiljevic about this telegram on the 19th, after midnight, when he came to Negoslavci, the house that you were staying at. On that occasion, did you get any instructions from him as to where you should provide security for those 2.000 persons for the exchange?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, I said then to Mr. Vasiljevic that we provided the kind of security that we could provide then for the people who surrendered at Mitnica, and that it would be very difficult to provide security for that many people. He said to me, "Sljivancanin, I sent professional people who know what the tasks are. You are supposed to cooperate with them. They have been through thick and thin. Do your best to carry this task out together." He did not make any special reference to 2.000. He probably knew the figure of people who had been taken prisoner better than I did, figures for the entire JNA. There were many people who were taken prisoner then. Just think of the scenes from the Bjelovar barracks, when, on the 3rd of October, the commander of the brigade was killed and when an enormous group of soldiers was taken prisoner in those barracks, and so on and so forth. I believe that Aca Vasiljevic was guided by that. It's not that we had a particular discussion as to it having to be 2.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You mentioned this group that came to conduct selection or triage of these prisoners of war, and that was from the security administration. In actual fact, was that the task of that group, that you had only assisted?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the moment they arrived that evening, they primarily took over the focus of this attack in terms of finding the perpetrators of the crime, and we cooperated with regard to all matters, as I have already testified here. I did not go beyond what they had asked me to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Yes. In your evidence, you said that at one point in time, when, on the 20th of November, you were in the hospital in Vukovar, Colonel Vujic said to you that you should stay in the hospital, that you should check the people who were still there, and that he would regulate the transport of crime suspects, their transport to Sremska Mitrovica. Have I interpreted this properly?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is the way it was. Perhaps I made a mistake at some point as I was talking about this. But when the colonel assessed that there was no further work to be done in the hospital, and when he saw that the military police and we, the security organs of the Guards Brigade, are doing our work properly, carrying out the tasks that we came there to accomplish, he left. If I can repeat his exact words, more or less, he said, roughly, "Sljivancanin, I am going to Velepromet. You stay here until the end, until this work is carried out." And he said that he would regulate the rest, that is to say, what was still to be handled at Velepromet. At that point, my understanding was that those people who would additionally be found in Velepromet as crime suspects and who would be brought from other parts of town that were still being searched - different basements, different buildings - as well as these people who were brought from the Vukovar Hospital, they would organise a single convoy and, during the course of the day, all of them together would be transported to Sremska Mitrovica. That is what I meant. If I misspoke, I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, please, this group of officers from the security administration, did it actually have authority given to them by the Supreme Command to carry out what you said just now, that is to say, to select people for this transport and to have them escorted to Sremska Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what they did on the evening of the 19th, and the only thing was that the transport of these people, that is to say, the vehicles, were organized by the command of the 1st Military District through our logistics assistant commander, that is to say, of the Guards Brigade. I really do not know enough about this; how many buses and other equipment what unit gave. The logistics assistant commander knows about this better than I do and Colonel Mrksic knows about this better, too. I really am not aware of all of these details who had to do what.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could Mr. Vasic please keep his microphone off while the witness is speaking. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I will switch off my microphone. The interpreters have asked me to keep the microphone switched. As far as the technical aspect of matters is concerned, I think everything is fine now and I think that we can play this footage, 1D42, an excerpt from 1D42. This is a TV programme of the Croatian television. The programme is called Latinca. So can we watch it a bit of it, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Later on I'll ask that this be translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: But let us first establish whether the witness is familiar with this or not, so that we know whether we need to elaborate on it or not.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the footage that I remember seeing on Croatian television last year. This was broadcast in the programme called Latinica, on some other programme. But at any rate, last year, they discussed the Vukovar events for two nights in these TV programme.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is the Latinica TV programme devoted to the issue of whether Vukovar was betrayed, and it has to do with the October events that you gave evidence about.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now play this footage and could I ask the interpreters to interpret the subtitles. I think they are rather clear and not going too fast, and there are only several sentences.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] Listen, there are not enough; right? What we have must be sufficient. Are we going to pull out the civilians? No, no, no. How are you going to do it? How are you going to pull them out? No. Therefore, do you know what conditions they are putting, sir? No, no, that's out of the question. Yes, I agree with you about it, but I would just like to remind you that there are 2.000 children there. What are we going to do about these children? All right. All right. I am still here. You do your job and I'll go and inquire about this. No pull-out can be discussed, not at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, I'd like to thank the interpreters for the effort they invested in interpreting what was said.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sljivancanin, do you recognise the speakers in this footage?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The man in the camouflage uniform is the so-called Mile Dadekovic, aka Jastreb, who, at the time, was the commanders of the paramilitary forces in Vukovar, and the other voice is the Croatian president, Mr. Franjo Tudjman.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: In this conversation, Commander Jastreb wants to pull out the civilians and President Tudjman does not allow that; correct?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. And this also reminded me about another occasion when Mr. Marin Vidic told me that children had been taken out of Vukovar to the coast, or something like that, in July of 1991. And he also complained about what the Croatian government did, because they wanted to remove the children out of Vukovar before combat started; however, they didn't allow that. They said that the children needed to come back and that allegedly they would serve as a shield. They would ensure that they would not be attacked. This is what Marin Vidic said. However, I have to tell you, when we reached certain basements in Vukovar, as we swept the terrain in order to ensure that there were no members of the paramilitary formations there, we came across some members of the ZNG who said that they had told civilians that they had to stay in the basements because the JNA would come and slaughter them. So when these civilians saw that we were there to help them, they were surprised. So there were cases like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I now tender this footage into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 844, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sljivancanin, we spoke about the cable you received from the security administration, and you said to Mr. Lukic, you described the circumstances of how you received this cable from the communications centre of the brigade. Were there other instructions from the chief of the security organs of the Ministry of Defence that you received in the same way as this cable, or were some other means of communications used, or rather, did you use the same centres of communication?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received very little information through the communications centre. One of such pieces of information was this cable, and perhaps I received another one or two such requests throughout the entire combat operation. Everything else arrived by mail, in writing.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Does this mean that these cables were urgent, because they were not sent through this regular channel, in writing?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it means that it was urgent. We were surprised ourselves. We had very few soldiers at the time, and we did not expect that the paramilitary formations would surrender in Vukovar on that day, at least it was a surprise to me and I believe the same is true of others.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When answering the questions of Mr. Lukic, you described the evacuation on the 18th from Mitnica. You gave evidence, saying that the members of Croatian paramilitary forces who surrendered their weapons at Mitnica were sent to Ovcara because it was nearby, and that on the 20th of November, the persons who had been separated in triage as suspects were not supposed to go to Ovcara. This is why I'd like to look at the entry in Exhibit 375, which is the war log of the 80th Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the entry made on the 19th of November, at 1800 hours. This is page 10 in English and in B/C/S ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure what the question is going to be, although I suspect I have an idea, but the war log relates to the 80th as opposed to -- as far as I'm aware, that's the document my learned friend is referring to. And, as far as I understand, this witness has no responsibility, as he says, to that particular brigade. That's the first objection I would make, and the second is it's leading the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the question is leading because it arises from the answer that Mr. Sljivancanin gave. I agree, but I am just now turning to the inquiry that was sent to the 80th Motorised Brigade by the Superior Command and Mr. Sljivancanin can simply tell me whether he knows about this or not. I think that it is proper for that type of question to be leading. However, I haven't yet found the page number in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, you may put to the witness whether he does know about this, but you will leave it to him to tell you what he does know about, if he does.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Your Honour. Thank you. So could we please put on the screen Exhibit 375, the entry made on the 19th of November, at 1800 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sljivancanin, can you please read this to yourself. You don't need to read it out loud. We've already read it several times here in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's hard for me to read this handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I'll try to do that and you can follow. "In the morning hours, the imprisoned Ustashas were taken to the prison in Sremska Mitrovica. Combat continues only in the sector of the hospital where the surrender of the remaining members of the ZNG and MUP is expected (about 200). Thus, it was ordered that we be on alert in order to organise the guarding of the prisoners." Do you know anything about such an order; namely, that the command of the 80th Motorised Brigade should be ready to organise the security of the prisoners who were supposed to come from the hospital to the sector of this brigade?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see this entry made on the 19th of November, at 1800 hours. I saw this war log for the first time here in the courtroom, or rather, I received it as a document upon arriving to The Hague. I did not have occasion to see it previously. The first thing I need to say is that on the 19th, in the afternoon, as I have told you, sometime after 1500 hours - although I'm not sure about the time - I was at the hospital with the representatives of the International Red Cross and I did not observe that there was any combat. As for this entry, in addition to receiving reports of the security organs, organs for morale, guidance, and logistical support, he also received reports from his subordinates and other commanders. So I cannot explain this entry. I don't know whether Mr. Mrksic issued any assignments to the commander of the 80th Brigade about this issue because I wasn't present, so I can't provide any additional information about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I was about to say that it's perhaps the right time for our second break. I am nearing the end of my examination and I would require a couple of minutes to, perhaps, review my notes and I may get rid of some of the questions and hence conclude earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It is a bit early, Mr. Vasic, and because of the earlier break for Mr. Moore, we're going to run out of tape time before 7.00. We don't want to squander time. Do you think that we should -- that it's important now for you to have the break at this moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours. Let's continue for an additional ten minutes - I think that's what we have left - and then we can break afterwards. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sljivancanin, when speaking of participation in creating and accompanying the convoy of civilians and the wounded, you said that it was in the jurisdiction of the logistical units of the 1st Military District. Did I understand you well?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on the information I had available at the time, I know that after the 18th, the assistant commander for logistics of the 1st Military District, General Zeljko Simanic, was present there with quite a number of officers from that logistics organ, and I believe that they were quite active in ensuring transportation means and providing assistance for evacuation of the people from the area of combat operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: This convoy of the wounded was led by a representative of the cabinet of the Federal Secretary, Colonel Nebojsa Pavkovic; correct?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You told us that the convoys with civilians, as well as this one with the wounded, were supposed to travel via Nustar, across the Croatian territory, and we know that later on the route was changed. Can you tell us, why was that? And how come these convoys did not travel via Nustar towards Vinkovci, if you know?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first time that the paramilitary formations of Croatia decided to surrender, an order arrived from the Superior Command which was conveyed to us by our commander, Colonel Mrksic, and it said that there were three centres where people from Vukovar were supposed to go. One was in Sid, arranged by the Red Cross; the second one was the prison in Sremska Mitrovica; and the third were agreed locations towards the Republic of Croatia, where the separation of forces was conducted. I know that the convoy from the hospital was supposed to go to Nustar, and as far as I can remember, but I'm not entirely certain because this was dealt with by Colonel Pavkovic, in the evening, I heard that they did not want to accept that convoy and that it went to Sremska Mitrovica. On the 19th, or rather, the night between the 18th and the 19th, the convoy led by Major Skoric, which is to say, that within the staff of the brigade in Negoslavci, through the communications means with the Superior Command, they always made arrangements, because we didn't have direct contact with Croatian authorities; it was done through the 1st Military District. So it had to be agreed with them where these people needed to be sent. Usually, the Chief of Staff would designate somebody from the operations organ to lead the convoy, and the 1st Battalion of the military police would provide escort. And, once again, they refused to accept this convoy, and then after much ado, it was returned back to Ovcara, as I've already said to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you know that on the following day, on the 20th, in the morning, once that convoy left from Ovcara towards Nustar, it was fired upon by the Croatian side? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that later on at the command post. I personally wasn't involved. I just heard about it because it was discussed. And later on I also heard it from Colonel Pavkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now we are going to turn to the portion of your evidence where you said that the original plan was that people who had been considered suspects were to be transferred to Sremska Mitrovica, but that Colonel Vujic, on the 20th of November, believed that it was better for them to go to the barracks. Did I understand you well?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The position was that all citizens, if I may call them that, all civilians, who had not surrendered as members of the paramilitary formations with weapons, in which case we didn't know whether they had committed any crimes or not, were supposed to go to Velepromet from Vukovar and that whole area; and only Mitnica, which did not gravitate towards Velepromet, in order not to create a lot of commotion, only Mitnica gravitated towards Ovcara and those people went towards those facilities. On the 20th, in the morning, when I met with Colonel Vujic at the gate of Velepromet, where he ordered me to report in order to go to the hospital together, I suggested, and I demanded, that these people that had gone through our triage were not supposed to go through the same process at Velepromet, but that it would be best for them to it go temporarily to the barracks until the convoy for Sremska Mitrovica was ready to set out, so that we could find other people that were supposed to join that convoy. The colonel had nothing against it. It was simply an arrangement made that morning in order not to trouble these people twice, to conduct the triage twice.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Was your suggestion approved by Colonel Vujic?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. We agreed on this together.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, is this a good time now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I only have a couple of questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sljivancanin, now I should like to go back to that part of your statement which refers to the 20th of November, when you say you arrived at the command post in Negoslavci and when, as you said, from Colonel Mrksic, you learned what the further tasks of the Guards Brigade were and that a government session had been held and, as you said, that they had taken over the group of suspects. Tell me, please, were you present at the regular briefing, reporting on the 20th of November, or did this take place after that regular briefing?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not -- I did not attend any meetings at the command of the Guards Motorised Brigade either on the 18th or the 19th or the 20th, in the afternoon. I was discharging the operational tasks of the security organs at that time, so I'm not aware of what meetings were being held, and, at any rate, I did not attend any.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I just have to explain the position of my client. He believes that you do not remember well and that he couldn't say that the government took over these suspects on that day. I shall now read to you, in respect of the conclusions from that session, what was said before this Tribunal in another case, the Dokmanovic case, by one participant in that meeting, namely, the Prime Minister Goran Hadzic. And that is on pages -- rather, on page 3124 of the transcript ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, we have both Mr. Moore and Mr. Lukic --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: May I let Mr. Lukic go first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You're so generous, Mr. Moore. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps I should have deferred to Mr. Moore. I have nothing against the asking of questions, but perhaps now I wish to raise something which is much more of a formal issue. I'm against the presentation to witnesses of transcripts of other persons, in principle, generally speaking. During the OTP's case, we established some rules of the game, which I believe we have all fully respected. Sometimes we could have said that someone was saying or had said something and we strictly paid attention not to make any reference to the name of the person being quoted during our examination, and the OTP actually asked us to abide by that principle. But it seems as if the rules of the game have been confused a bit as we went along, and certain persons, who have not even taken the stand in the Tribunal, are being quoted, i.e., their statements are being presented. Of course, I agree that those who were present in the court are quoted - that is okay - but I am generally against the reading of statements of other persons. So what I'm saying: I would prefer if this were interpreted in his own words, if something is being claimed by another person was interpreted in his own words. And Mr. Sljivancanin is familiar with the testimony given by Mr. Hadzic because he has received the relevant material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: At the moment, of course, we don't have any testimony from Mr. Hadzic. Now, Mr. Moore, is there anything ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes. Firstly, it is cross-examination and, from my memory, the rules of the game, as they're being called, that my learned friend should not lead the witness on a topic, but, I would submit, more importantly, it is the way that the matter should be put. Mr. Sljivancanin says he was not there on the 18th, 19th, and 20th. It seems to me that Mr. Mrksic is saying that that may be incorrect. If that's what is being said, it should be put directly to Mr. Sljivancanin that, on behalf of Mr. Sljivancanin -- on behalf of Mr. Mrksic, Mr. Sljivancanin is incorrect; that he was there on such a such a day and that on that day a topic was mentioned in the presence of Mr. Sljivancanin. That means, therefore, that Mr. Sljivancanin knows the area; that he is able to answer in relation to it; he can either agree or deny. As matters stand, the way it has been put, from my part, I fail to see the logic of its presentation, so I would suggest it has to be put clearly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Moore. Now, Mr. Vasic, are you adapting your position in view of the helpful comments of your colleagues, or do you want me to give you a few more helpful comments?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I'm going to rephrase my question, but I think that my position has not been understood very well by my colleagues. My position was that Mr. Mrksic claims that he did not say to Mr. Sljivancanin that the persons who were suspects were taken over by the government of Eastern Slavonia, and I wanted to support that by a fact stemming from a statement made by Goran Hadzic, which he made before this Tribunal. In that statement, he claims that the meeting was attended by a lieutenant colonel who said that any surrender was out of the question. That is the point of what I wished to put to this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, that isn't evidence that's been given in this trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. Indeed, it was given in the Dokmanovic trial, not in this trial.
