utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, I would suggest to you, Mr. Vasic, that you should go no further than to suggest that in another trial evidence was led that whatever it is precisely that you want to say, and then have the witness see whether that reminds him that that could be the case or whether he disagrees with that evidence or what is his position. But you can't dress it up any higher than that, and that is Mr. Lukic's matter of principle, as I understand it. And we're somewhere approaching Mr. Moore's point, but I think he was off on a slightly different one. Yes, Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I am precisely going to stand on the ground that you just delineated. I fully agree with what you just said.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You heard what was being said, Mr. Sljivancanin. Does this refresh your memory? Was this information somewhat different 15 years ago; namely, that they were not handed over?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not hear what Hadzic said during his testimony. I read a great deal of material and many inaccurate, untrue statements. I claim with full responsibility - I am looking everyone square in the eye here - I know not 100 per cent but with 1 million per cent certainty that I was at the commander's on the 20th, in the evening. As for the government session, before hearing about it from the commander, I heard it from my security officer, Srecko Borisavljevic. I don't want to repeat that. I told you what he said. And I fully stand by what I said; that that was said that evening at the command post.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could Mr. Vasic please keep his microphone off while the witness is speaking. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you that I was surprised when Srecko Borisavljevic said to me that these persons, instead of being taken to Mitrovica, were taken over by the government of Slavonia, Baranja and Western Srem/Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we please have a look at Exhibit 843, if possible. That is 3D1665; it was a 65 ter document, that is. Page 2. Thank you. Could you please enlarge the fourth paragraph. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sljivancanin, you are aware of this document, aren't you? It's the report of the 10th of December. Or do you want me to show you the first page?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No need. I'm aware of this document; I know this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Your positions were presented here in relation to what the government was doing, and it says here: "The command of the Guards Motorised Brigade was compelled to carry out mobilisation of personnel in the zone of combat activities as well and to include them in the fighting in Vukovar. The response of personnel was very low, especially in the village of Negoslavci. The few people who did respond to call-up remained on their positions for two or three days. On the whole, the majority of the Serb population in the zone of combat activities OG South was not ready for participation in battle and they all wanted to guard their village, house, or the like. Such conduct and this poor call-up was mostly contributed to by the government of SO Slavonia, Baranja and Western Srem. That same government appointed, as commanders of staffs of the Territorial Defence, persons who were not respected or held in high regard by the population because of what they had done previously, as well as persons who were in high positions and who were corrupt and who had 'proven themselves' in dirty deals and dirty business. "At one of the meetings of this government (none of the members of that government appeared in Vukovar practically until the liberation), attempts were made to diminish the success of the units of the JNA, and Prime Minister Hadzic figured in that most prominently. The feeling of the majority of the population towards the government and its representatives is bad." Mr. Sljivancanin, can you agree with me that, in this report, you included events from the government meeting held on the 20th of November, in Velepromet, when you said that they were trying to diminish the success of JNA units?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have testified here and I said that Srecko Borisavljevic told me about what Bogdan Vujic had told him about in terms of that government session, and the way I understood it then was that their attitude towards us, members of the Yugoslav Peoples' Army, was practically negative, too. In addition to that, this attitude of certain members of the government was negative during the course of our stay in that territory, and I wrote about that in my counter-intelligence estimates. As a matter of fact, I was compelled to bring people in for interviews. When I was given the task to carry out operational work towards this Minister of the Interior that I had brought in for an interview, he left the town. I personally, at that time, did not feel that it was right, and I did not go by that; namely, to have any kind of organs established that were not in accordance with the constitution of the Socialist Federalist Republic of Yugoslavia. That was my position then, that is what I wrote then, and I think that I wrote this briefly but in very realistic terms.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Yet again, we have great trouble hearing the witness if other microphones are on. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise to the interpreters because of the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You will agree with me that in this report that you submitted at the request of the head of the department you did not state that the government of Eastern Slavonia, Baranja and Western Srem took over a number of certain persons on the 20th of November. That is not written in this report of yours; right?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said here that I wrote this report on the 21st and sent it to the administration or department. You had occasion to see many other counter-intelligence reports that I had sent; I showed them here. I did not copy anything from those other reports in the new reports that I wrote. I thought there was no need for repetition. Now it's easy to be a general after the battle, as the saying goes. Had I known that I would be here, facing the Hague Tribunal, perhaps I would have written a great many other things in my report as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you say, after that report on the 21st of November, did you get any instructions from the security administration regarding that report and questions raised in that report?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I did not get any instructions, except for what I said. When, together with the chief of security of the cabinet of the Federal Secretary, I, after returning from Vukovar, went to see the head of the administration, he suggested certain questions to me regarding which I should have written a report, and I did that to the best of my ability, and no one raised any objections at that time. Whether they read this, whether they looked at this, what they did, I don't know. But they did not ask me to do anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I would like us to comment upon the following: A document which is marked 3D050171.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is 3D38 in terms of the 65 ter documents. Can we please have it on the screen. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sljivancanin, do you know what this is and whether that is the document that has yet another document attached to it, including information about members of paramilitary formations of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know what this is. This is a document of the chief of security of the cabinet of the Federal Secretary, dated the 10th of November, 1991, about information concerning members of the National Guards Corps and the MUP in Vukovar. And he is instructing us what we should do in professional terms, in terms of specialist direction, that is to say, us, the security organs. And it is addressed to the security organ of the Guards Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would now like to ask for the second page to be displayed; namely, the report. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sljivancanin, this is actually the document that was submitted, attached to the previous document that we saw, and it includes information about the paramilitary formations of Croatia that are supposed to be a guideline for the work of security organs.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably, if this document was attached to the previous document.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Yes. And it was admitted as 826; I see that now. Thank you. Tell me, as for these guidelines that you received, you acted in accordance with them, right, after having received this document? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whenever I would receive this kind of document, I would make the commander aware of it and the assistant commanders, too, as well as some commanders, for example, the commander of the battalion of the military police, if he can -- or if they can give me information that would be important for us, the security organs. And we worked, in operative terms, we, the security organs, on the basis of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Now, I would like to ask that we see document 3D050912; 3D39, as a 65 ter document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Could we please have the document identification number again.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. 3D050192; 3D39 is its 65 ter number. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sljivancanin, are you familiar with -- is this document familiar? Take a look at it.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is one of the reports on the security situation in the Guards Motorised Brigade which was compiled on the basis of the report of the security organ of the Guards Motorised Brigade by the chief of security of the cabinet of the Federal Secretary and sent to the security administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we take a look at the end of this page, and zoom in on it, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: This last sentence says: "In work on processing prisoners of war, the organ of security of the Guards Motorised Brigade was suggested --" rather, "it was suggested to the organ of security of the Guards Motorised Brigade to adopt a selective approach focussing on the detection and identification of war criminals and documenting of war crimes; the identification of foreign mercenaries; the elucidation of the objectives and intentions; the documenting of the conjunction with the foreign factor; the documenting of espionage activities in favour of foreign intelligence institutions; the collection of important intelligence on the disposition, strength, armament, and intentions of the enemy forces; and the creation of conditions for the operational combining or planting of misinformation. "We shall regularly report on the situation of security in the Guards Motorised Brigade and the measures undertaken."

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: These are guidelines from the department of security and the cabinet of the SSNO, sent to the security organ of the Guards Motorised Brigade; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And it is according to these guidelines that you acted.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We tried. We did our best to act upon these guidelines. If you have read any of the reports that I sent, you could have seen that, in our reports, we actually referred to the individual cases that we had detected, which does not mean necessarily that our reports were always correct. This was preventive work on our part, and all the information that we arrived at was there. As data from a number of sources are collected in one centre, later, if two or three pieces of information should coincide, then they would provide concrete guidelines as to what is to be done in the operative work directed to certain specific individuals. So if you look at any of my reports, you can see that there are a lot of names that we listed there, giving their secret names, what we had learned about them, including the work of foreign mercenaries or some persons that have been infiltrated into the territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that you have said to us, if I understood you correctly, that all this data that was ultimately collected by the security administration filtrated, verified, is then again returned to the security organs for further action. Did I get you right?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The security organ cannot charge anyone, nor can it immediately consider someone an enemy or the perpetrator of a crime unless it has collected detailed and reliable information on that person. That is why the work of the security organ is laborious and it is answerable for its actions should it charge anyone incorrectly. I'm sorry that we, perhaps, might have suspected some person without concretely proving it, because that requires further processing, further work, to see what the ultimate outcome would be. So these are some elements that I regret, but it was so. Our members, the troops and the officers of the Guards Motorised Brigade, as far as they were concerned, we had precise and correct data; and we knew if charged someone, why we were charging that someone. But it was difficult to follow suit in the territory, generally speaking. That is why the collection, the screening of perpetrators, of suspects, of suspected perpetrators of criminal offences, was a very serious exercise. We didn't come to a person and say, "You have killed someone," or so. We would just have people who were suspects and we were suggested to detain such persons as briefly as possible, and then to send them, during combat operations, to Sid, where the investigative authorities were working, and then also as soon as possible to Sremska Mitrovica, where the competent investigative authorities were in operation, for them to actually deal with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Your Honours, at this point, I should like to propose that this document be tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 845, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Sljivancanin, for your answers. That ends my cross-examination, Your Honours. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vasic. Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Sljivancanin.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: In giving your testimony here, you said that you regularly toured the units of the Guards Motorised Brigade on the front line, did you not?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, every day, from morning, and sometimes even at night I went to the positions where some units were and I spent the night there. But I spent most of my time with the Guards Brigade troops at the front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you be so kind, then, as to tell us: To what extent were you familiar with the tasks of the Assault Detachment 1 and Assault Detachment 2? Were you familiar with the direction of operations of these Assault Detachments, with their war disposition, combat disposition? And were you familiar -- could you observe any problems that they were encountering, and how?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was always present at the command post whenever a decision was being taken on the use of units of the Guards Motorised Brigade. I endeavored, I did my best, to remember as much as possible to which unit the commander had issued some specific tasks, because I was interested in that, as the chief of security, whether the commanding officers were correctly honouring their obligation, i.e., executing their tasks. And also, if I considered that the decisions of the commander were not being respected, I also wanted to let the commander know about that. I always knew what particular assault detachment had -- what task it had. Initially, there were three assault detachments; later, I believe that there were five. And I was aware of what their missions were.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us, from this time distance, what was the task of JOD -- of the Assault Detachment 1 and that of the Assault Detachment 2?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can. Assault Detachment 1, according to the decision of the commander, should move along the direction, the street of Svetozara Markovica to the settlement of Bosko Buha and then to Milovo Brdo. And along this axis it was to disarm paramilitary units, dismantle the obstacles, the barricades, and clear the roads to enable free passage, free movement. And Assault Detachment 2 was to go through Sajmiste Street and then on from Dalmatinska Street towards the water tower, lift the siege, the blockade, on the barracks, disarm paramilitary formations along that direction, remove the barricades, and create the necessary, i.e., normal, conditions for the city. And initially, the assault detachment -- Assault Detachment 3 was to go from Vucedol through Mitnica and to break out at the water tower.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us what assault detachment took Milovo Brdo, and in which time period was that?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say that Assault Detachment 1 reached Milovo Brdo and cleared that part of town of all those who were opening fire on the troops and on members of the Yugoslav Peoples' Army. And I remember that that was, perhaps, on the 9th or 10th of November, because at that time a colonel from the General Staff, who I believe was a Croat, asked me to find the person, if I could. He gave me the name of that person who -- that was his brother's daughter, in fact; and to send her to Sid. And I had a lot of problems about that and I asked people to help me out, and that is why I remember the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should like to ask Your Honours for Exhibit 430 to be placed on the screen, but that is the only one that I will be showing. So, Exhibit 430, the last paragraph, please. Not the first one, the last. Thank you. Number 4. Would you be so kind as to zoom in on the last paragraph, please, a bit more. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sljivancanin, could you please read this under "Tasks." You have a task under item 4, if you could, please read it for us.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says here under item 4: "Assault Detachment 1, without the 1st Motorised Battalion, from the current area of combat disposition, to be transferred to the axis Dalmatinska Street to Alija Alijagic Street, and then to the water tower. "Task: In direct conjunction with the 2nd Battalion of the military police and Assault Detachment 4, take features within the scope of streets Alija Alijagic, the Stjepan Supanac school, and reach as soon as possible the area of Slavija (the water tower) from which point prevent the possible pull-out of Ustasha forces from the Mitnica axis."

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I ask now, Your Honours, as the witness has read this, to place Exhibit 156 on the screen, and to zoom in on the central part of town, as much as possible, to enlarge it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before this comes up on the screen, may I add that this document that I'm now reading --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, you don't have to. Thank you very much. We want to be specific. Please don't mind my interrupting you, but I wish to expedite proceedings. Can you please zoom in on the centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Is this enough for you, Mr. Sljivancanin, what you can see on the screen, for you to be able to show on this map how it is that you perceived the task of Assault Detachment 1 and the units acting in concert with it? Can you show it on this map?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is sufficient. I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I ask the usher to provide Mr. Sljivancanin with a pen so that he could show it to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is how it was. This here is Sajmiste Street. Should I mark it with a number?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: I don't think there is anything on the screen.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I am marking it with a red line.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: That is okay.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is Sajmiste Street.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Well, you can put number 1 and then circle it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This here, next to 1, this red dot here, that is the barracks. Should I encircle it?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, you may encircle it, and where the barracks is, put a number 2. But slowly, please.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. This here is the barracks. That's number 2. This here is Dalmatinska Street.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Mark it with number 3, but I believe this is not the readily visible on the screen.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This here is Dalmatinska Street. Of course, I can tell you where the other streets are; Radnicka, Svetozara Markovica, the water tower. Here is the water tower, number 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: And Milovo Brdo is this area here, as far as I can recall, number 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you, on the basis of what you have drawn in this map, explain to us this mission of Assault Detachment 1 and the units acting in conjunction with Assault Detachment 1, to explain to the Court what that mission looked like.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this task which I just read, it is stated that the Assault Detachment 1, without the 1st Motorised Battalion, should be transferred to the axis Dalmatinska Street, marked by 3, and the water tower, and should act there in conjunction with the 2nd Battalion of the military police and Assault Detachment 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Before I ask for this to be admitted into evidence, can you tell us whose decision was it to use the units in this way, as you have described just now?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was just about to tell you. As here, this was frequently referred to as an order. It was not an order, it was a decision, a decision of the commander of the Operations Group, for the execution of an immediate task. The commander changed his decisions. When he saw that he failed the first time, he organised his forces differently the next time around.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Whose decision was it, then?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was Commander Mrksic's decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can we tender this map into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 846, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We won't be needing the usher's assistance any longer. No need to draw anything else. And now a question for Mr. Sljivancanin:

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know, Mr. Sljivancanin, whether Captain Radic was at the hospital on the 18th of November, 1991?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The last time I saw Captain Radic in Vukovar was when the units of the 1st Motorised Battalion reached Milovo Brdo. On the 18th, I wasn't in the hospital myself. I believe that none of the members of the Motorised Guards Brigade were at the hospital on that day, because, based on the information that I have, our 1st Motorised Battalion, on the 19th at some point, entered the hospital. The documents can confirm this, but I can't tell you anything further about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us whether Captain Radic was with you at the hospital on the 19th when Borsinger was there with you?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm telling you again: The last time I saw Captain Radic was at Milovo Brdo, and I don't remember, that is to say, I didn't see him, or rather, he wasn't with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking for a direct answer to my question. On the 19th of November, 1991, did you order Captain Radic to arrest Dr. Njavro in the morning hours, between 8.00 and 10.00 a.m., or at any other time during the day?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Captain Radic was commander of the motorised company within the 1st Motorised Battalion. I had absolutely no powers to issue orders to him, nor did I order anything to him. Mr. Njavro was not arrested. Pursuant to my decision on the 20th, Mr. Njavro was taken from the Vukovar Hospital to Sremska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And at the same time, did you issue any other order to Radic to arrest the male nurse called Ante Aric; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never issued such an order, nor was I authorised to issue any orders to Radic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Specifically, did you order, on the following day, Captain Radic to return the aforementioned person back to the hospital, or not?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not true either.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On the 20th of November, 1991, you were at the hospital. My question is: Did you, at any point in time during that day, in the morning hours, issue an order of any sort to Captain Radic to conduct a selection or to search, with his soldiers, for the men who were moving towards the buses on Gunduliceva Street, by telling him the following, and I'm quoting: "Captain Radic, search these prisoners"?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is completely untrue. Neither was I authorised, nor did I see Radic there. The search of the soldiers within the hospital was done by the members of the 2nd Battalion of the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the reference for my last question is page 9732, line 14 through 17, the evidence of Witness P030.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sljivancanin, did you order Captain Radic to take Njavro and Ante Aric to the barracks on the 20th, at any point during the day, or not?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never issued such an order to Radic. On the 20th, in the morning, after the consultation with Mr. Aco Vasiljevic, Tumanov issued an assignment to my assistant for counter-intelligence tasks, Mladen Karan, and Captain Bozic from the military police to escort four persons to the prison in Sremska Mitrovica. And I gave you the names of those four.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, line -- page 69, line 5 is recorded as a question whereas, in fact, it was the answer provided by Mr. Sljivancanin. Page 69, line 5, that entire segment is the answer of Mr. Sljivancanin. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Did you, at any point in time, and specifically on the 20th of November, order Captain Radic to return from the barracks 15 to 20 men to the hospital who were members of the medical staff or were related to the medical staff?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never issued such an order to Captain Radic. The list of the medical personnel was sent by me, by my driver, to the barracks to my assistant Vukasinovic Ljubisa, and pursuant to my request, he returned persons from that list to the barracks on the 20th, as I have told you, between 11.00 and 12.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Sljivancanin, did you at any point in time issue any sort of an order to Captain Radic, or not?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never had occasion, nor was I capable of issuing any order to Radic. I saw him as any other company commander. It was my duty to tour him and to have a conversation with him that I was entitled to as a security organ, in order to find answers to questions from my jurisdiction, about the location of soldiers, the weapons, and disposition of paramilitary formations in the axis of his company.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: When you say "the disposition of paramilitary formations," do you have in mind Croatian paramilitary formations?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Did you have any kind of a command post at Vuteks, or not?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I explained to you the deployment of my organs in Negoslavci. I never had any sort of a command post or -- what did you call it? You call it a warehouse at Vuteks? No, nothing of the sort.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Thank you, Mr. Sljivancanin, I have no further questions. Your Honours, I have concluded my examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Borovic. Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Mr. Sljivancanin, when one talks about the security organ, and I try and use ordinary language, would it be fair to say that it could be described as the eyes and ears of the command in security areas and advises the commander when necessary?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, it could not be put that way, that it's the eyes and ears. That is one of the organs, according to establishment, of a brigade and it first appears in the brigade command according to that formation. As for the purview of its tasks and its work that I have already spoken about here, those are prescribed by the rules of service of the security organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: No. Please just answer the question. Security organ, it's the eyes and ears of the command, isn't it? It watches what is going on. That is its function; that is its purview, as you describe it.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I am telling you, once again: The security organ is a professional organ of the commands and institutions that has tasks from the field of state security in terms of protecting the constitutional order and the constitution of the state and uncovering hostile activities vis-a-vis a unit and within a unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: What do you mean by "uncovering hostile activities," if it isn't acting as eyes and ears of a command or commander?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, hostile activities are everything that jeopardises law and discipline and the combat readiness of units; namely, criminal offences, discipline, and concealing such acts if they are not reported on through the chain of command; that is to say, all are duty-bound to take care of security in the units, starting from squad leader, platoon leader, company leader, all the way up to the commander of the brigade, and the soldiers themselves within a unit. The security organ leader should, through his own activity and the application of certain methods of work, should - how should I put this? - prevent things from happening, if one does not know that this is going on within a unit because it's being done in a secret way, and even if there are persons who are infiltrated into a unit with regard to a particular matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: That's exactly what I am suggesting. It is not a passive organisation. It is capable of being passive but its function is also active and proactive. That is correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you, I cannot go outside the purview of my work to explain some kind of theory of security organs. I spent a short period of time working in security organs. It was my understanding that this is one lines of this security function, taking care of these tasks that I already mentioned to you. There's no need for me to repeat them again. But everyone in a unit, from the commander onwards, is in charge of security.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But the security organ is a specifically-designed - and I will use the ordinary English word - it is a specifically-designed unit to assist a commander in finding out what may be going on which would be detrimental to that command. That is your task. It's certainly one of your tasks, I would suggest. That's its purview; that's its reason, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, that's not the way it is. A security organ is not there to discover everything that is going on in a unit. Then there would be no other officers and there would only be a security organ. A commander receives reports according to the chain of command and the security line and moral guidance and logistics. So the security organ is one of these elements taking care of the compactness of the unit and that it acts within the purview of its tasks. The way you put it, there should only be --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't mean to interrupt. The security organ adds an additional element to the function of what I will call "everyday officers," doesn't it? Otherwise, it has no purpose at all. That's right, isn't it? It's an additional element.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every officer in the structure of the unit, as envisaged by the Yugoslav Peoples' Army, is important in his own right. I cannot single out anyone, including security organs; say that a security organ is more important to the brigade commander than, say, his chief of staff or his logistics assistant commander. It depends on the tasks involved. Everybody is important in his own right, and they make up this compactness that is in the interest of the combat-readiness of that unit, so that it would be as it should be, so that the unit carries out the tasks assigned to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: That's very well. We will have to go through, regrettably, some of the exhibits. Let me just look at this, then, from a common-sense point of view. In 1991, we know over 200 people were murdered, innocent people murdered, and buried in Ovcara. You are, as you say, an innocent man, but whether you like it or not, you have been indicted and stand trial for that. Who do you consider is responsible for the murder of these innocent people? You must have thought about it.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, it is a great shame and it is highly inhumane on the part of those who killed those people, murdered those people. That was done by cowards. It really -- if I knew who did it, I would have told you. I would tell you here and now, but I did not have occasion to deal with this in detail. I heard everything that you heard here, too. That event occurred - I showed you here - in the zone of responsibility of another unit and at a time when the members of the Motorised Guards Brigade were exhausted, very tired, and when they could hardly wait to get some rest after a mission accomplished. And this was perhaps the most sensitive period, when there is a change-over of duty among units including us, a replacement of units. And one should talk to the people who were in that zone and who testified here to the effect that they did know something about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I will ask the question again. You know perfectly well that it's been suggested that you were in charge of OG South, but I am asking you, categorically - we know about the perpetrators - but who was actually responsible for the murder of these innocent people at Ovcara? Are you saying it's the government? Are you saying it is Panic? Are you saying that it is Mrksic? Are you accepting it's yourself? Who is responsible?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never said that it was the government or Panic or that it was Mrksic. I have imparted to you the information -- I have here imparted to you the information that I knew then, and I believe that the collection of all the testimonies, all the evidence presented, can actually result in a finding of who actually perpetrated that heinous crime. I really don't know. Now, to give you some just suppositions on my part, I am here as a witness to tell you my truth or about what happened then, what I know happened then, and that is what I'm doing. It is very hard for me to say or judge who did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, that is not correct, I would suggest to you, because what you are saying, is it not that, firstly, Ovcara is not in your zone of responsibility? That's one of the things you are saying, ergo, it's not my fault. It's not my zone of responsibility; it's not my fault; I'm not to blame. You are also saying that you heard that it was handed over to the government and then we now know that people were killed. So I'm asking you, as the innocent man that you say you are, when an indictment was issued in 1995, you must have been racking your brain, saying, "What on earth happened? Who is to blame for this?" So what is your answer?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, really, really, when I heard about it, I was extremely distressed and I was extremely sorry, and it is, indeed, the height of abomination that those people should have been killed. And, as I have said in my introductory remarks here, this inflicted great damage and a great blot on the honourable members of the -- members of the Yugoslav army who only wanted to actually carry out their oath, their constitutional oath, to preserve Yugoslavia. And now these people have to bow their heads and, because of those murders, cannot even say that they were in Vukovar because of this dirty business that was perpetrated by somebody else. I have not undertaken any investigations, but I contend this was not a zone of responsibility of the Motorised Guards Brigade. We did not commit those crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: It's certainly the zone of responsibility of OG South; that is correct, isn't it? The answer is just yes or no, Mr. Sljivancanin.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, overall, this entire area was the operational zone of Operations Group South, but it is primarily in the zone of responsibility of the actual unit in whose ambit it is, and the commander of that unit is responsible. We can say, generally speaking, that it was the zone of the 1st Military District of the entire Yugoslavia, but that, then, would be correct. But then other units and other commanders would not be necessary if it were just up to one person.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Mr. Sljivancanin, you have made great noises about honesty, looking people in the eye, being truthful. The reality is that this is in the zone of responsibility of OG South; that's right, isn't it? Can we have yes or no on this?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have replied. If it is accepted that such a group existed, I am not excluding that it was not its zone. But first it was the zone of the battalion and then the battalion is in the zone of the OG and then it is the zone of the Military District, generally speaking. So what I'm telling you is that the first responsible is the directly -- the commander directly responsible for the zone of the immediate unit, and then we go on along the chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I will ask the question one more time: Ovcara is within the zone of responsibility of OG South; that is correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, in a nutshell, very briefly, Ovcara was first in the zone of responsibility of the 80th Motorised Brigade at the time when it is alleged here -- when it is said here that this crime happened, and the zone of the 80th Motorised Brigade comprised the zone of the OG South.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We had three clear questions and three clear answers. This is my comment. I believe, really, that if Mr. Moore asks this question for a fourth time -- Mr. Sljivancanin was quite clear in his first reply, and then the question was repeated and then the answer was repeated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I know the answers were repeated, Mr. Lukic. Carry on, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can we take it, then, that this level of honesty, directness, precision and integrity that you say you are going to display in court, that the answers you have given are a representation of that? Is that what we are to expect?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I am doing my best to say what I know, in keeping with how I was brought up and reared, and not to withhold anything from you. Mr. Moore, according to our military rules, every commander is, first and foremost, responsible for his own zone, so I'm telling you the zone in which Ovcara was on the 18th, 19th and 20th, first and foremost, was the zone of the 80th Motorised Brigade, and that zone belonged to the zone of OG South.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Let's deal with it, then, a different way, if that's the way you are going to answer. Let us take a situation, and a hypothetical situation, that OG South is in the zone of responsibility for Mr. Mrksic. Can we just deal with that for a moment. You don't disagree, I presume?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Mrksic, if he was issued orders, although I did say here that we were drawn attention then not to refer to the establishment name of the brigade, but I accepted that that was a secret name for the Guards Brigade as well, and I never, in my appearances, ever referred to the Guards Brigade in Vukovar. So, if he was appointed the commander by an order, then he was the commander of the OG South and he was answerable for the zone of Operations Group South.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I try and abbreviate that? Is that answer saying Mr. Mrksic was responsible for his zone of responsibility, which was OG South? Is that correct? Is that what you're saying, in shortened form?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, if he had the such orders and then appointment to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And if a commander of a zone of responsibility is informed that criminal acts are occurring within his zone of responsibility, he is under a duty to, at the very least, investigate what is occurring; do you agree with that? Yes or no, please.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And, in accordance with his duty, it is also right to say that if there is a criminal act which is occurring, he should use such force as is necessary in all the circumstances to stop that criminal act occurring. That, also, is correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If he should learn that in the zone of the OG South, which is a large zone, any crimes are being committed, he should order first to the commander of the zone where such criminal offences are being perpetrated, be it the brigade, what measures are to be taken in order to prevent such crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I will ask the question again. How he does it is a matter for conjecture. But it is right, is it not, that a commander should use such force as is necessary in all the circumstances to stop that criminal act occurring. That is correct, isn't it, as a general principle?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The general principle would be that the -- for him to ask the commander in charge of the area where such crimes have been committed to take steps to prevent it. If that commander was unable to do that by himself, then to help him; and if he cannot help him, to ask for assistance from the Superior Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So can I take it that the answer is yes?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've given my reply. Please don't hold it against me, but I really should not like to answer with just a yes or no, as in a quiz. I've explained how this was regulated by our rules then in the Yugoslav Peoples' Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your rules are quite clear on the matter, I would suggest - and I will deal with it tomorrow - but the reality of the situation is that if an incident occurs, a criminal act occurs, within a zone of responsibility of a commander, that commander has a duty to intervene to stop the criminal act. You've already agreed to that; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have agreed, we have agreed, that it is his duty to intervene and request from the specific person responsible for the zone where the crime is being committed to take measures. If he cannot, to help him; if he cannot help him, to seek further assistance from the Superior Command. I think I have been clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, let us just take that one step further. You say it is for him to request from the specific person responsible for the zone where the crime is being committed to make measures. The superior commander, in this case, Mrksic, has an ongoing duty to ensure that the measures that are being taken are adequate and appropriate to stop the criminal act occurring; that is right, isn't it? He can't just issue an order and walk away with blind eyes, can he?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. The commander, if he has issued an order, he should actually see to it that that execution -- that that order is executed to the full. He should certainly control whether it has been carried out to the full.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And how does he control to the full? Explain to this Court the techniques and methods and systems that a commander can put into place for that.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, a commander, if he issues a task to a subordinate commander to the effect that he should deal with a problem in his zone for which the former has learned exists, shall seek from the latter feedback information to the effect whether the problem has been dealt with, resolved, to be informed by that subordinate commander. Secondly, a second way, he can personally go to the unit, the subordinated unit, in question and verify whether the problem has been resolved; or he can issue a written order and assign an officer from the command to go to the subordinated command, to control and verify how the subordinated commander has executed the tasks issued him by the superior one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And why would it be important for a commander to go personally to the unit to verify whether his order is being carried out or not?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my view - this is from my standpoint - it is not necessarily correct. I, as the commander, was very often to go and verify whether certain tasks that I had issued were, indeed, being executed, whether they had been dealt with properly, and, at the same time, to also gain personal insight into the attitude of the commander in question vis-a-vis the orders which I issued him; of course, when weather permitted and conditions generally. If I was unable to do that, I was entitled to send certain officers from my own command whom I empowered to carry out that control. But when the task is very important, it is much better for the commander, in person, to check how his orders are being carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: If a commander was informed that, through the day, there had been abuses and that there was a probability of not only grievous injuries but also death occurring to prisoners of war, would you, in your judgement, as a professional officer, consider it desirable for personal attendance to that subordinate unit?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If the superior commander had such information, I believe that any commander would, and I would, go and see whether something like that was, indeed, taking place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to move on to a different topic and I wonder, even though it's slightly early in the evening, whether it would be possible to conclude 12 minutes early and continue tomorrow morning. I can, however, continue if you wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Because of our adjusted timetable, you have only three minutes left, not 12 or 13, and if you're moving to a new topic, this would be a convenient --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- time. We'll resume tomorrow, in a different courtroom, at 9.00 in the morning. I think it's Courtroom II. We'll adjourn now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
